name: PID controller (ISA / standard)
description: A PID controller in the ISA (standard, ideal) form, u = P·(e + (1/I)·∫e dt + D·de/dt): P is a gain, and I and D are times in seconds (the integral and derivative times, often written Ti and Td). An I of zero or less turns the integral term off, and a D of zero or less turns the derivative term off. Use the parallel block if your controller reports Kp, Ki and Kd. A node with its own C++ program: it holds the control signal and the error as states, and reads the setpoint, gains and limits from live shared parameters. Point its Measurement input at the state to control, and connect its Control output to what it drives.

nodes.name: PID controller (ISA / standard)
nodes.description: A PID controller in the ISA (standard, ideal) form, u = P·(e + (1/I)·∫e dt + D·de/dt): P is a gain, and I and D are times in seconds (the integral and derivative times, often written Ti and Td). An I of zero or less turns the integral term off, and a D of zero or less turns the derivative term off. Use the parallel block if your controller reports Kp, Ki and Kd. Wiring: the controller reads the quantity to control from its Measurement input. Open the node's Program and point that input at the state of the node you want to control (any node's state can be chosen), or leave it on this node's own Measurement state and drive that state yourself. The Control output state holds the control signal, recomputed every step; connect a relationship from it to the node being controlled (for example, an edge whose equation uses the controller's output as a heat flow, force or voltage). The Error state shows the setpoint minus the measurement, for plotting. Setpoint, gains and limits are shared parameters: the setpoint and gains are live, so they can be moved with a slider during a run, and each live parameter's slider range is editable in the parameters table. Both output limits and the derivative filter are constants. Output limits apply only when the maximum is larger than the minimum. The derivative acts on the error, so a step in the setpoint produces a brief kick in the output; a filter time greater than zero softens it. The integral stops accumulating while the output is held at a limit and the error would push it further (no wind-up), and the controller's memory is saved with checkpoints, so forks and resumed runs carry on exactly.
